notes.meaning: God calls everyone who is spiritually thirsty to come to him and receive life and refreshment. These blessings are pictured as nourishing water, milk, and wine, which cannot be bought with money because they are completely free gifts. God warmly welcomes anyone who senses their deep spiritual need to receive his salvation.

differ.view: Methodists view the wine and milk as the specific inward blessings of the gospel, especially peace, joy in the Holy Spirit, and the love of God.

notes.meaning: God asks why people waste their hard work and money on things that can never nourish the soul. Chasing worldly pleasures and false ideas leaves the human heart hungry and dissatisfied. When people listen closely to the Lord, they receive the rich spiritual food that brings true peace and joy.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some nineteenth-century critical scholars understood the food and drink not as spiritual blessings, but as the rich physical food awaiting the exiles upon their return to their homeland.

notes.meaning: The Lord invites his people to listen attentively to him so their souls may truly live. He promises to make an everlasting covenant with them, which is a sacred, unbreakable agreement. This promise gives them the reliable, loving mercies first given to King David, which find their fulfillment in Christ.

differ.view: Calvinistic Baptists teach that God must give spiritual life to a person first before they are able to hear and come to Christ in faith.
Methodists teach that this covenant was established through the death of Christ for all people, offering eternal blessings to all who choose to come.

notes.meaning: God explains that he set up King David as a leader, but the words look forward to the Messiah, Jesus Christ. Christ acts as God's faithful witness who speaks the truth and rules over all peoples. He lovingly guides everyone who follows him in the way of righteousness.

differ.view: Some premillennial evangelicals believe this refers to the literal King David, who they believe will be raised from the dead to rule an earthly kingdom during the millennium.

notes.meaning: The Lord tells the Messiah that foreign nations outside Israel will eagerly run to him. People who once lived without the true God will now join his family. This happens because the Lord has glorified his Son, especially by raising him from the dead.

The prophet urges people to seek the Lord in prayer while the door of opportunity is still open. God draws especially close to people when his message is being taught and his Spirit is working. We should call on him right away, because a time will come when this day of grace has ended.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern language studies point out that the Hebrew phrase means seeking God while he allows himself to be found or makes himself available.

notes.meaning: God commands sinners to turn away from their evil habits and their wrongful ways of thinking. When people return to the Lord, he promises to show them deep compassion and to pardon them completely. Forgiveness gives us a fresh start and restores our relationship with God.

differ.view: Reformed Baptists emphasize that the thoughts sinners must abandon include any idea that they can earn right standing with God by their own good deeds.
Methodists stress that returning to God requires sincere repentance and faith that leads directly to a newly reformed life of ongoing obedience.

notes.meaning: The Lord explains that his thoughts and ways are completely different from human thinking. Human beings are often slow to forgive when someone hurts them, but God is always ready to forgive sinners who turn back to him. We can come to him with confidence because his mercy is far greater than ours.

The enormous distance between the skies above and the earth shows how far God's ways rise above human ways. His wisdom, purposes, and willingness to show mercy are far higher than our limited ideas. Remembering how high God's thoughts are helps us trust his plans even when we cannot fully grasp them.

Rain and snow fall from the sky and do not leave until they have watered the ground. This moisture causes crops to sprout, providing bread for people to eat and seed for farmers to sow for next year. In nature, God makes sure his rain never fails to do the job it was sent to do.

Just like the rain and snow, the words God speaks will never fail to achieve his intended goals. His promises of redemption and forgiveness will always bring about the exact results he planned. God's message has power to soften hearts and will never return to him empty.

differ.view: Reformed commentators note that while God's promises are completely dependable, individuals can still hinder the fruit of the word in their own lives through unbelief.
Some Baptists apply this verse to Jesus Christ as the living Word of God, who came from heaven and returned to the Father having successfully gathered a harvest of redeemed people.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: A popular modern reading uses this verse to say that quoting Scripture guarantees people will receive what they ask for, though teachers caution that God's word accomplishes his goals rather than human desires.

notes.meaning: God promises that his people will leave their spiritual captivity in peace and celebration. The prophet pictures hills bursting into song and trees clapping their branches to join in the gladness. This joyful scene shows the deep freedom and relief that come when God redeems his people.

Painful thorns and prickly briers will disappear, and beautiful cypress and myrtle trees will grow in their place. This transformation pictures how God takes a ruined, sinful life and fills it with spiritual beauty and goodness. This wonderful work serves as an everlasting sign that brings honor to the Lord's name forever.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the miraculous growth of trees as a permanent, literal physical renewal of the desert rather than merely a poetic picture of spiritual change.
